summary: Defines a DNS resource record type called APL for lists of address prefixes. It gives a way to describe networks or address ranges in DNS. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: It lets the phone book list whole neighborhoods, not just single houses.

questions: how to publish ip ranges in dns
subtitle: A DNS record type for publishing lists of IPv4 and IPv6 address prefixes.

tldr.problem: DNS had no standard way to publish lists of IP address prefixes or network ranges in a machine-readable format, forcing ad-hoc solutions like TXT records or zone file conventions.
tldr.mechanism: APL RR defines a new DNS record type 42 that stores a list of address prefixes. Each item specifies an address family (IPv4 or IPv6), a prefix length, and optionally a negation flag to exclude ranges.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now query DNS for formatted lists of address ranges, enabling uses like publishing organization network blocks, classless delegation, access control, and multicast group addresses in a standard format.

today: RFC 3123 is experimental and remains so. Although the APL RR is registered and can be used in DNS, it has not achieved broad adoption because no single application semantics became standard. The flexibility of the format—where each application defines its own meaning—prevented the network effects needed for widespread use.

sections.title: The APL Record Type
sections.content:
The APL (Address Prefix List) RR is a new DNS resource record type assigned the numeric value 42 by IANA. It allows DNS to store lists of IP address prefixes, where each prefix represents a range of addresses. Unlike the A record (which stores a single IPv4 address) or AAAA record (which stores a single IPv6 address), APL can hold multiple prefixes in one record.

APL records are defined only for the Internet class (IN) of DNS records. An APL record with empty content is valid and represents an empty list. Multiple APL records can exist for the same domain name, and their interpretation is left to the application using them.
sections.eli5: APL is a new type of entry in the DNS phone book. Instead of writing down one phone number, you can write down a range of them, like "all numbers from 555-0100 to 555-0199 belong to the sales department."

sections.title: The APL Data Format
sections.content:
Each APL record contains zero or more items. Each item specifies an address family (identified by a 16-bit number assigned by IANA; 1 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6), a prefix length (the number of bits to match), a negation flag (to exclude a range instead of including it), and the actual address bytes. For IPv4, the address part is 0 to 4 octets; for IPv6, it is 0 to 16 octets. Trailing zero octets are omitted to save space.

The items in an APL record MUST be kept in order and MUST NOT be rearranged or merged by DNS servers. This preserves the semantics defined by the application using the record. For example, an access control list might rely on the order of rules.
sections.eli5: Each item in the list tells you whether to include or exclude a range of addresses. You write the first bits of the address, and the prefix length tells you how many bits matter.

sections.title: Writing and Reading APL Records
sections.content:
In a DNS zone file, an APL record is written as example.com. IN APL 1:192.168.0.0/24 2:2001:db8::/32. The 1: prefix denotes an IPv4 address family, and 2: denotes IPv6. The address and slash-prefix syntax mirrors CIDR notation. A negation is written by preceding the item with an exclamation mark: !1:10.0.0.0/8 means exclude the 10.0.0.0/8 range.

The RFC provides example APL records for various uses: publishing an organization's address ranges (like RFC 1101 did with TXT records), describing zones covered by classless delegation, restricting DNS zone transfers to certain IP ranges, and grouping multicast addresses. Each application must define what the prefix list means in its context.
sections.eli5: You write the addresses using a simple text format, with a number and slash to show how many bits matter. A `!` in front means "not this one."

sections.title: How Applications Use APL
sections.content:
APL defines a framework but not specific meanings. The RFC states that any application using APL records MUST include documentation on how to interpret them. This includes what the prefix list means, how to handle negations, what to do with empty lists, which address families are expected, and how to treat address families not yet defined.

Security concerns arise because APL can disclose network topology information. Using APL to construct access control lists could expose internal network structure to potential attackers. Applications using APL should weigh this risk and apply appropriate DNS security measures like DNSSEC or TSIG (transaction signature).
sections.eli5: Different applications can use APL for different purposes. Each one has to explain what the list means and how to use it safely.

sections.title: Deployment and Status
sections.content:
RFC 3123 is experimental. APL records have seen limited adoption, as the specific application semantics have not been widely standardized. DNSSEC deployments in some regions have defined how to use APL for publishing delegation signer (DS) records in a machine-readable format, but broader adoption has remained limited.

The record type is registered and available in DNS implementations that support it, but applications must define their own interpretation and handling rules. The flexibility of the format—allowing any application to define its own semantics—is both a strength (general-purpose) and a weakness (no standard semantics, limiting interoperability).
sections.eli5: APL exists and you can use it, but there is no widespread agreement on what the lists should mean in most applications, so it has not become common.

fields.name: Address Family
fields.desc: IANA-assigned family number: 1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Number of bits in the address part (0-32 for IPv4, 0-128 for IPv6).

fields.name: Negation
fields.desc: 1 if this item is negated (excluded), 0 if included.

fields.name: AFD Length
fields.desc: Number of octets following (0 to 4 for IPv4, 0 to 16 for IPv6).
